Font Effects in Charts

Bold, Italic, and Beautiful

Published

October 20, 2025

Modified

October 24, 2026

1 Setting up R Packages

library(tidyverse)
library(ggformula)
library(sysfonts) ## use custom fonts (need to be installed on your OS)
library(systemfonts) # Thomas Pederson's recent font management package
library(showtext) ## add google fonts to plots
library(ggtext) ## add improved text rendering to ggplot2
##
library(ggrepel) ## Text-repelled labels
library(marquee) ## Annotations with fonts in ggplot

2 Introduction

We have used a _setup.qmd at our Project root to enable ggplot/ggformula themes, with fonts.

We are now ready to use markdown effects in ggplot titles, text, and other places. We will use the ggtext package by Claus Wilke to achieve these effects, and {marqee} package by Thomas Lin Pedersen.

Data

We will work with a familiar dataset, so that we can concentrate on the chart aesthetics, without having to spend time getting used to the data: the penguins dataset again, now part of the R installation!

Basic Plot

A basic scatter plot first, which we will decorate with font effects: ( We will use our _setup.qmd right from the outset here. )

Show the Code
p1 <- penguins %>%
  drop_na() %>%
  gf_point(body_mass ~ flipper_len, colour = ~species, size = 2) %>%
  gf_labs(title = "My Penguin Plot", x = "Flipper Length", y = "Body Mass (gms)") %>%
  gf_refine(
    annotate(geom = "text", label = "Important\n Points", x = 220, y = 3500),
    annotate(geom = "rect", xmin = 200, xmax = 210, ymin = 3000, ymax = 5700, alpha = .2),
    annotate("curve",
      x = 220, y = 3200, yend = 3000, xend = 205,
      linewidth = 1, curvature = -0.5, arrow = arrow(length = unit(0.5, "cm"))
    )
  ) %>%
  ## Labels and Title
  gf_labs(
    title = "Weight vs Flipper Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (Pygoscelis)",
    subtitle = "A scatter plot of Body Mass versus Flipper length.",
    caption = "Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) PLoS ONE",
    x = "Flipper Length (mm)",
    y = "Body Mass (gm)",
    color = "Species"
  )

p1

3 Using {ggtext}

From Claus Wilke’s website → www.wilkelab.org/ggtext

The ggtext package provides simple Markdown and HTML rendering for ggplot2. Under the hood, the package uses the gridtext package for the actual rendering, and consequently it is limited to the feature set provided by gridtext.
Support is provided for Markdown both in theme elements (plot titles, subtitles, captions, axis labels, legends, etc.) and in geoms (similar to geom_text()). In both cases, there are two alternatives, one for creating simple text labels and one for creating text boxes with word wrapping.

Importantgridtext package issues

NOTE: on some machines, the ggtext package may not work as expected. In this case, please do as follows, using your Console:

  • remove gridtext: remove.packages(gridtext).
  • Install development version of gridtext: remotes::install_github("wilkelab/gridtext")

3.1 element_markdown()

We can use our familiar markdown syntax right inside the titles and captions of the plot. element_markdown() is a theming command made available by the ggtext package.

element_markdown() → formatted text elements, e.g. titles, caption, axis text, striptext

Show the Code
p2 <- p1 |>
  ## New code starts here: Two Step Procedure with ggtext
  ## 1. Markdown formatting of labels and title, using asterisks
  gf_labs(
    title = "Weight vs Flipper Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins (*Pygoscelis*)",
    subtitle = "A scatter plot of Body Mass versus Flipper length.",
    caption = "Data: Gorman, Williams & Fraser (2014) *PLoS ONE*",
    x = "**Flipper Length** (mm)",
    y = "**Body Mass** (gm)",
    color = "Species"
  ) |>
  ## 2. Add theme related commands from ggtext
  ## render respective text elements
  gf_refine(theme(
    plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    legend.title = ggtext::element_markdown(face = "bold") # Works
  ))

p2

3.2 element_markdown() in combination with HTML

This allows us to change fonts and font-effects in titles, labels, and captions:

Show the Code
## use HTML syntax to change text color
p2 |>
  gf_labs(title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins <i style="color:#28A87D;">Pygoscelis</i>') |>
  gf_theme(
    plot.title = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10)
  ) # trbl
Show the Code
## use HTML syntax to change font and text size
##
p2 |>
  gf_labs(title = 'Bill Dimensions of Brush-Tailed Penguins <b style="font-size:32pt;font-family:Tangerine;color:#28A87D;">Pygoscelis</b>') |>
  gf_theme(
    plot.title = ggtext::element_textbox_simple(
      fill = "yellow",
      padding = margin(4, 2, 4, 2, "pt"), # trbl
      halign = 0
    ),
    plot.caption = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.x = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    axis.title.y = ggtext::element_markdown(),
    plot.margin = margin(t = 10, r = 10, b = 10, l = 10)
  ) # trbl

4 Using {marquee}

marquee is stated to be a future-proof, full-Markdown supporting too for font effects in ggplot and text. It sets up the use of ( at least ) three very useful functions:

  • geom_marquee() and geom_marquee_repel(): a ggplot geometry for text effects;

It supersedes both geom_text() and geom_label() in its capabilities, and even if you don’t need to plot rich text, the styling of geom_marquee() is much more capable.

  • element_marquee(): much like what we saw with ggtext (element_marquee( family = NULL, colour = NULL, size = NULL, hjust = NULL, vjust = NULL, angle = NULL, lineheight = NULL, color = NULL, margin = NULL, style = NULL, width = NULL, inherit.blank = FALSE ))

  • marquee_grob(): which allows us to create an aribitrary grob (graphical object) with rich text, which can be used in any ggplot2 annotation.

Let us try a few examples to see its capabilities. For full understanding, head off the to the marquee reference webpage. We will once again decorate our original vanilla plots with marquee elements.

5 Wait, but Why?

  • Using appropriate fonts in our plots can make them more readable and visually appealing.
  • Font Effects may be useful to draw attention to very specific parts of a complex plot.

6 Conclusions

In this module, we have learned how to use custom fonts in our ggplot2 plots using the showtext package.
